evals.prompt: Define Blue Ocean Strategy in 2-3 sentences. Include value innovation, new demand, and why differentiation plus low cost matters.
expected_elements: Names W. Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne or the Blue Ocean Strategy framework
Explains creating uncontested market space or new demand
Explains simultaneous differentiation and low cost
Does not define the method as ordinary competitor avoidance

evals.prompt: Explain the mental model of Blue Ocean Strategy. Name at least 6 primitives and describe how they connect.
expected_elements: At least 6 of: strategy canvas, value curve, factors of competition, buyer utility, price, cost, adoption hurdles, noncustomers, alternatives, ERRC choices
Explains how eliminate/reduce fund cost change
Explains how raise/create lift buyer value
Explains that a new value curve must be commercially viable

evals.prompt: Why does this skill exist for agents? Name the failure modes it prevents.
expected_elements: Prevents calling ordinary differentiation a blue ocean
Prevents competitor benchmarking with a blue-ocean label
Prevents raise/create-only overengineering
Prevents ignoring noncustomers and commercial viability

evals.prompt: Distinguish Blue Ocean Strategy from Five Forces, Seven Powers, Playing to Win, framework-fit-analysis, and prioritization. Give a mechanism-level reason each neighbor is different.
expected_elements: Five Forces diagnoses industry structure and profit pressure
Seven Powers classifies durable firm-level power
Playing to Win formulates integrated strategy choices
Framework-fit-analysis chooses which framework to apply
Prioritization ranks a known queue of work
Blue Ocean Strategy reconstructs value curves and market boundaries

evals.prompt: Place Blue Ocean Strategy among strategy frameworks. What upstream inputs can feed it, and what downstream outputs can follow it?
expected_elements: Classifies it as market-creating strategy / value innovation
Names upstream inputs such as customer/noncustomer research, alternatives, industry canvas, or Five Forces
Names downstream outputs such as a value curve, ERRC grid, experiments, strategy cascade, or execution goals
Keeps it distinct from moat diagnosis and task prioritization

evals.prompt: Give an analogy for Blue Ocean Strategy that preserves value-curve reconstruction. Then name one bad analogy and explain what it gets wrong.
expected_elements: Uses an analogy involving changing the game board, map, market boundary, or rules
Maps old competition factors to old rules or old terrain
Maps ERRC choices to the new value curve
Rejects a bad analogy that treats the method as mere avoidance or generic creativity

evals.prompt: Novel scenario: A crowded project-management app says it will create a blue ocean by adding more AI features and lowering price. Apply Blue Ocean Strategy by diagnosing what is missing and proposing a better next analysis step.
expected_elements: Rejects feature addition plus low price as insufficient
Requires a strategy canvas or current factors of competition
Requires noncustomer or alternative-industry insight
Applies eliminate/reduce/raise/create logic
Tests buyer utility, price, cost, and adoption
Labels assumptions rather than inventing certainty
